doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Internet access to music and the marketing of 'smooth jazz'
summary: Easy access helps only if you know what to look for; jazz is used as a marketing label.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you think there’s a difference in what you did back then as — I mean you were a student of the music, even while you were teaching. And you had to go to these lengths of what you just described. Nowadays everything’s under your fingers and is available at a moment’s notice, and I’ve been trying to figure out whether this is good or bad or both.

Well I think it’s like the Internet, it’s both. It can save you a lot of time, but unfortunately it can only save you a lot of time if you know what you’re looking for. If you don’t know what you’re looking for you will probably waste more time than any people in the past just going through a lot of stuff that’s completely useless and it’s not about the music at all. And that’s the problem. I think today the most important thing, the most useful thing a good jazz instructor could do for a student is, well first of all to give them a capsule version in terms of recordings and artists and specific pieces of music of what some of the most important jazz recordings are to understand what jazz really is. Because I think one of the problems in recent years has been the NAMM jazz has been used to market so many kinds of music that don’t have anything to do with jazz at all and it’s just this kind of catchy marketing tool. And the most obvious one in recent years is so-called smooth jazz. And I remember in the early sixties, besides the fact that there were only four TV stations then and there was way more jazz and classical music and theater and opera and all kinds of stuff on those four channels than we can probably find on 150 channels on cable today. But in those days there were only a half a dozen categories of music. There was classical, jazz, pop and folk. That was about it. Then you had rhythm & blues. And
since then there’s still one category for jazz basically, and there’s about twenty categories for pop music. That’s dumb and dumber.
